header: Electric-car charging (the cost of a charge is in tariff.ts): I give an approximate idea of how long a battery of a given size takes to charge (say from 10% to 90%) from AC and DC chargers of various ratings, and what the battery and charger specifications mean. Pure; nothing is stored or sent anywhere. The method is the plain one, and the answer is marked as approximate everywhere it is shown: energy to add (kWh) = capacity x (to% - from%) AC charger: the car's on-board charger sets the pace, at the lower of the charger's and the car's AC limit; about 90% of the power reaches the battery. DC charger: the power is the lower of the charger's and the car's DC limit, about 95% reaches the battery, and a lithium-ion battery takes less as it fills: up to 50% about 75% of that peak on average, 50-80% about half of it, above 80% about a fifth. Cold weather, a hot battery or an old one make it slower still.

behaviours: AC: 40 kWh from 10 to 90 percent (32 kWh) on a 7.4 kW point takes about 4 h 48 min
AC: the car's on-board charger limits a bigger charger (7.4 kW car on a 22 kW point is no faster)
AC: a car that takes 22 kW charges three times faster on a 22 kW point than on 7.4
DC: more charger power is faster until the car's own limit, then no faster
DC: 10 to 80 percent of 40 kWh at a 50 kW peak is 40 to 60 minutes (the usual figure of makers is about 40 to 60 for cars of this size)
DC: the last stretch is slower: 80 to 90 percent takes longer per kWh than 10 to 50
DC is much quicker than AC for the same battery
